course.learn: AAA is a sequence for controlling and recording access. Authentication proves identity, authorization decides what that identity may do, and accounting records activity.
course.why: Separating these functions prevents “being logged in” from automatically meaning “allowed to do everything,” and it preserves an audit trail.
course.example: A user signs in with MFA, receives read-only access to a database based on role, and every query is logged.
course.exam: Identity = authentication. Permission = authorization. Activity record = accounting.

slides.title: Authentication
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Authentication is the process of proving an identity. Factors can be something you know, have, are, do, or somewhere you are; MFA requires factors from more than one category.
course.why: If attackers can impersonate legitimate users, every later access-control decision becomes unreliable.
course.example: A user enters a password and then approves a hardware-token challenge.
course.exam: Do not confuse authentication with authorization. Authentication answers “who are you?”

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Determining what an authenticated identity is allowed to access or do.

course.learn: Authorization determines what an authenticated subject is allowed to access or do. Models include DAC, MAC, RBAC, and ABAC.
course.why: A valid identity still should receive only the permissions needed for its role or attributes.
course.example: Two employees authenticate successfully, but only the HR employee is authorized to open payroll records.
course.exam: Authorization comes after authentication. RBAC uses roles; ABAC evaluates attributes; MAC uses centrally enforced labels; DAC lets owners grant access.

breakdown.explanation: Access control restricts which subjects can access which resources and what actions they may perform. ACLs express allow/deny rules on objects, interfaces, or network traffic.

slides.title: Accounting
slides.raw:
Accounting
Monitors resource usage
Generates logs
Helps identify unauthorized access attempts
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Recording activity through logs, audit trails, and session records.

course.learn: Accounting records how identities and systems use resources. Logs, audit trails, session records, and usage data support accountability and investigations.
course.why: Without records, defenders may know an incident happened but not who did what or when.
course.example: A VPN gateway records login time, source IP, session duration, and bytes transferred for each user.
course.exam: If the question asks about tracking or recording activity, think accounting/logging.

breakdown.explanation: Continuously observe activity or state so abnormal behavior, drift, or failure can be detected early.
